newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans 1997 budget gap at 4.5 pct of GDP. [CORRECTED 00:42 GMT 25/2]
newsitem.headline: Romania plans 1997 budget gap at 4.5 pct of GDP. [CORRECTED 00:42 GMT 25/2]

text.p: Romania's government has drafted its 1997 budget with a deficit of 4.5 percent of gross domestic product, down from last year's figure of 5.8 percent.
A copy of the budget, made available to Reuters on Monday, showed indicators within guidelines provided by the International Monetary Fund.
It put 1997 budget revenues at around 70.4 trillion lei, with spending at some 80.9 trillion lei, yielding a deficit of 10.5 trillion lei.

It gave no dollar equivalents for budget figures. Romania's leu currency has been subject to sharp fluctuations in recent weeks. It was quoted on Monday on the interbank market at about 8,800 per dollar compared to 4,100 in the New Year.
The draft has yet to be discussed in a government meeting and then to be submitted to parliament for approval.

The government's figures apply to the "consolidated budget", which includes the state budget, local government budgets, social security expenditure, supplementary pension funds and various other extra-budgetary funds.
The bulk of 1997 consolidated revenues comes from profit and wage taxes, which totalled 40.2 trillion (corrects from 16.6 trillion) lei. About 10 percent of GDP is set aside for social security.
State budget revenues stand at 40.4 trillion lei and spending at 52.8 trillion lei.

The deficit figures were agreed during talks with the IMF and the World Bank. Both lenders withheld credits for the ex-communist country last year over foreign exchange market curbs and the overshooting of spending targets.
Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's government -- a coalition of mainly centrists and social democrats who ousted leftists in last November's elections -- has pledged to contain deficits.
Ciorbea said last week the bulk of the consolidated budget gap would be financed through external credits -- about 3.4 percent. The rest, he said, would be funded by domestic loans.
Romania is seeking around $1.0 billion in total loans from the IMF and World Bank to underpin its tough reforms.
Official estimates put year-on-year inflation this year at 89.5 percent against 56.9 percent in 1996, led by price liberalisation for fuel, electricity and food. ($=7,744 lei)
